page: Amazon Web Services g6f.large is an x86_64 server instance powered by the AWS Nitro hypervisor. It features a dedicated AMD EPYC 7R13 processor operating at 3.4 GHz, configured with 1 physical core and 2 vCPUs. The instance is equipped with 8.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core. For accelerated graphics and compute tasks, it includes a fractional NVIDIA L4 GPU with 3 GB of VRAM. Local storage consists of a 100 GB NVMe SSD, and baseline network bandwidth is rated at 2 Gbps.

Benchmark results indicate a divergence between single-core and multi-core performance. The stress-ng single-core CPU performance is strong, placing in the top 25%, whereas multi-core performance falls into the bottom 25%. Memory bandwidth is relatively constrained, with read-only small block cached bandwidth at 87.8 GB/sec and large block uncached bandwidth at 20.45 GB/sec, both ranking in the bottom 10%. Geekbench multi-core, software compilation, and ray tracing benchmarks also score in the bottom 10%. However, LLM inference speed for prompt processing using a medium 7B model achieves an average rating at 69.08 tokens/sec.

Given its hardware profile, the g6f.large offers a cost-effective entry point for GPU-accelerated workloads without the resource overhead of a full dedicated GPU. The inclusion of a fractional NVIDIA L4 GPU and 100 GB of NVMe SSD storage makes it suitable for lightweight graphics-intensive tasks, small-scale LLM prompt processing, and basic machine learning inference. It is less suited for memory-intensive databases or heavy multi-threaded compilation tasks due to its lower memory bandwidth and multi-core performance limitations.
description: Amazon Web Services g6f.large is an x86_64 graphics-intensive instance running on the Nitro hypervisor. It features a dedicated AMD EPYC 7R13 processor with 2 vCPUs (1 physical core) clocked at 3.4 GHz, 8.0 GB of DDR4 memory, and a 100 GB local NVMe SSD. Acceleration is provided by a fractional NVIDIA L4 GPU with 3 GB of VRAM. Performance benchmarks show strong single-core CPU capabilities, though multi-core and memory bandwidth metrics are relatively weak. The instance achieves average performance in LLM inference prompt processing for small and medium models. This configuration is qualitatively cost-effective for entry-level GPU workloads, lightweight graphics processing, and small-scale machine learning inference, while avoiding the higher costs of full-GPU instances.
